summary: Proposes JSON Type Definition (JTD), a format for describing the shape of JSON messages, with goals of code generation from schemas and portable validation with standardized error indicators. It is intentionally limited in power and is experimental. The document states it lacks IETF consensus.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON messages are like forms. JTD is a simple way to write down which boxes a form has and what goes in each, so computers can check forms and write code for them.

questions: how to validate json with a schema
what is json type definition jtd

subtitle: A JSON schema language designed for code generation and validation

tldr.problem: JSON lacks a standard, simple way to describe what shape a message must have, and existing schema languages are either too complex for code generation or too expressive to match programming language type systems.
tldr.mechanism: JTD (JSON Type Definition) provides eight schema forms—empty, ref, type, enum, elements, properties, values, and discriminator—that map cleanly to common programming language constructs, enabling portable schema validation with standardized error messages and reliable code generation.
tldr.outcome: Developers can write a JTD schema once and automatically generate code in multiple languages, validate JSON data with consistent error reporting, and avoid the overhead of schema languages more expressive than their target language.

facts.label: Schema forms
facts.value: 8 (empty, ref, type, enum, elements, properties, values, discriminator)

facts.label: Integer types
facts.value: int8, uint8, int16, uint16, int32, uint32 (no 64-bit)

facts.label: Error format
facts.value: JSON array with instancePath and schemaPath

today: RFC 8927 is Experimental and does not have IETF consensus. Its purpose is to gather experience with limited-expressiveness schema languages for JSON. Tools implementing JTD and code generators are available; the approach is in use by nodes validating or generating code for JSON APIs. If JTD proves successful and widely adopted, it may be brought to the IETF for further standardization.

sections.title: Why JTD Is Different
sections.content:
JTD is intentionally minimal. It does not try to describe every possible JSON structure. Instead, it covers the patterns most JSON-using applications actually need while matching the type systems of mainstream languages like C++, Python, Java, and JavaScript.

Existing schema languages like JSON Schema can express nearly any constraint, but that power comes at a cost: code generators cannot reliably emit idiomatic code, and implementations have to interpret complex semantic rules. CDDL can describe complex formats but is harder to write and read.

JTD takes the opposite approach: it intentionally omits features like 64-bit integers (which JSON transmits unreliably), regex patterns, and conditional constraints. This limitation makes JTD schemas easy to convert to type definitions in any programming language, and makes writing tools atop JTD straightforward.

The eight forms of JTD—empty (accepts anything), ref (reference to a reusable definition), type (primitive types: boolean, numbers, strings, timestamps), enum (one of a fixed set), elements (arrays), properties (objects with named fields, like structs), values (objects acting as dictionaries), and discriminator (tagged unions)—directly correspond to type system features in every mainstream language.
sections.plainLanguage: JTD is a simple way to describe JSON data. It does not try to describe complicated rules that real programming languages cannot represent. It focuses on the things that actually matter and are actually used.

sections.title: The Eight Schema Forms
sections.content:
Empty form ({}) accepts any JSON value and produces no errors. Use it when the content is unconstrained.

Ref form ({"ref": "name"}) references a schema defined in the root's definitions object, enabling reuse and recursion. For example, a user-location field can reference a shared coordinates definition rather than repeating it.

Type form ({"type": "uint32"}) constrains a value to a primitive: boolean, float32, float64, int8, uint8, int16, uint16, int32, uint32, string, or timestamp (RFC 3339 format). Integer types enforce range constraints; a uint8 must be 0–255.

Enum form ({"enum": ["PENDING", "DONE"]}) restricts a value to one of a fixed set of strings, mapping to enums in code.

Elements form ({"elements": {...}}) describes an array; the nested schema applies to every element. An {"elements": {"type": "uint8"}} schema accepts only arrays of bytes.

Properties form describes objects with named fields. Each field is either required (properties) or optional (optionalProperties), with a schema for each. An object like {"name": "Alice", "age": 30} might require name (string) and optionally have age (integer).

Values form ({"values": {...}}) describes objects acting as maps or dictionaries, where the nested schema applies to the value of every member. {"values": {"type": "string"}} accepts {"key1": "value1", "key2": "value2"}.

Discriminator form expresses tagged unions. A discriminator field (e.g., "event_type") holds a string tag. A mapping defines a properties schema for each tag value, so different event types can have different required fields. This maps to enums-with-associated-data in Rust or discriminated unions in TypeScript.
sections.plainLanguage: JTD has eight different shapes for JSON data. Empty means anything goes. Ref means use a definition from earlier. Type means a number or string or time. Enum means one of a few choices. Elements means an array. Properties means an object with named fields like a record. Values means an object used like a dictionary. Discriminator means pick a type by a tag.

sections.title: Validation and Standardized Error Reporting
sections.content:
A JTD implementation validates JSON data against a schema and, if validation fails, returns error indicators in a standardized format: a JSON array of objects, each with instancePath (a JSON Pointer to the part of the data that failed) and schemaPath (a JSON Pointer to the schema constraint that was violated).

For example, validating [1, 2, "not a number"] against {"elements": {"type": "uint8"}} returns an error with instancePath: "/2" and schemaPath: "/elements/type", precisely locating the problem.

This standardized format means all JTD validators report errors the same way, and applications can consistently handle validation failures. An implementation can choose to report all errors or stop at the first; either way, the format is portable.

All eight forms support a nullable flag; when set to true, null is accepted in addition to whatever the form normally requires. For instance, {"type": "string", "nullable": true} accepts both strings and null.
sections.plainLanguage: When data does not match the schema, JTD says exactly what was wrong and where in the data the problem is. All validators agree on how to report the error, so any program can understand it.

sections.title: Generating Code from Schemas
sections.content:
Because JTD is intentionally limited to constructs that exist in mainstream programming languages, a tool can reliably generate idiomatic code from a JTD schema.

For example, a JTD schema describing a user object with required name (string), age (uint32), and optional email (string) can be converted to a C++ struct, a Python dataclass, a Java class with getters, a TypeScript interface, or a Rust struct—all idiomatic and without manual tweaking.

The generator maps the eight forms to language features: properties become structs/records, values become maps/dictionaries, discriminators become enums with associated data (or sum types), enums become language enums, elements become arrays or lists, and type constraints become type declarations with range checks.

Because JTD does not include regex, conditional constraints, or other schema features that lack clear language equivalents, a code generator can always emit correct, idiomatic code without guessing.
sections.plainLanguage: Because JTD only describes things that programming languages have, you can write code from a JTD schema automatically in any language. If the schema says there is a field called name that is a string, the generated code will have exactly that.

sections.title: Metadata and Extending JTD
sections.content:
JTD schemas can include a metadata field holding an arbitrary JSON object with custom information not used in validation. Tools like code generators can read metadata to adjust their behavior: a code generator might use "metadata": {"pattern": "email"}" on a string field to emit an email validation helper, for example.

However, metadata is not standardized. Different tools may or may not understand different metadata fields. Parties sharing schemas should agree in advance on any metadata they will interpret, and metadata MUST NOT affect whether a schema accepts or rejects data—only validation rules do that.

This design reserves extensibility without compromising interoperability. A schema can include tool-specific metadata without breaking other implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Schemas can include extra notes for code generators, like instructions on how to format a field. But these notes do not change whether data is valid. Every tool agrees on what makes data valid; extra notes are optional.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Rationale
sections.content:
RFC 8927 is an Experimental specification and explicitly states it does not have IETF consensus. Its purpose is to gather experience with JTD as a practical schema language and to validate whether the constraint to map onto programming language type systems is the right trade-off.

The RFC omits features that other schema languages support. Appendix A explains two notable omissions: JTD does not support 64-bit integers (JSON transmits these unreliably; 32-bit integers and floats are recommended), and does not support non-root definitions (keeping definitions at the root prevents ambiguous recursion and complex resolution rules).

Appendix B compares JTD to CDDL, showing how the same data patterns are expressed in each language. Code generators, validators, and other tooling for JTD are available on GitHub at jsontypedef. If JTD proves valuable and widely adopted, it may eventually be brought to the IETF for standardization and refinement.
sections.plainLanguage: JTD is experimental and new. It intentionally leaves out some things to keep it simple and practical. If it proves useful, it may become a standard. Right now, people are trying it out to see if it works.

viz.caption: The eight JTD schema forms and their use

items.title: Type
items.text: Primitive values: boolean, integers, floats, strings, timestamps.

items.title: Enum
items.text: One of a fixed set of string values.

items.title: Elements
items.text: Arrays; validates every element against a subschema.

items.title: Properties
items.text: Objects with named required or optional fields (structs).

items.title: Values
items.text: Objects used as dictionaries or maps.

items.title: Discriminator
items.text: Tagged unions: a field picks which variant is present.

items.title: Ref
items.text: Reference to a reusable definition; enables recursion.

items.title: Empty
items.text: Accepts any JSON value without constraint.
